## Introduction

Tipping is a common part of eating out in the United States, and many diners say they tip a fixed percentage of the bill. This paper asks whether larger restaurant bills are related to larger tips.

## Literature Review

Etiquette guides have long promoted a "fifteen percent rule," which implies that tips should rise steadily with the bill [@gratuity2018]. However, some researchers argue that many diners tip out of habit, leaving similar amounts no matter what they spend [@servewell2022], so the strength of the link between bill and tip remains an open question.

## Method

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats

df = sns.load_dataset('tips')
df[['total_bill', 'tip']].describe()
```

Using `{python} len(df)` restaurant bills ranging from $`{python} f"{df['total_bill'].min():.2f}"` to $`{python} f"{df['total_bill'].max():.2f}"`, a Pearson correlation was computed between the total bill and the tip. The null hypothesis is that total bill and tip are not correlated (r = 0), and the alternative hypothesis is that they are correlated (r ≠ 0).

## Results

```{python}
corr_matrix = df[['total_bill', 'tip']].corr()   # 2 x 2 correlation matrix
r = corr_matrix.loc['total_bill', 'tip']         # row label, column label
r_test = stats.pearsonr(df['total_bill'], df['tip'])   # same r, plus a p-value
pval = r_test[1]
p_text = "p < .001" if pval < 0.001 else f"p = {pval:.3f}"

strength = "very strong" if abs(r) > .8 else "moderate" if abs(r) > .4 else "weak"
direction = "positive" if r > 0 else "negative"
corr_matrix
```

```{python}
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='total_bill', y='tip')
```

Total bill and tip showed a `{python} strength` `{python} direction` correlation, r(`{python} len(df) - 2`) = `{python} f"{r:.2f}"`, `{python} p_text`, so we `{python} "reject" if pval < 0.05 else "fail to reject"` the null hypothesis. In this sample, diners with `{python} "larger" if r > 0 else "smaller"` bills tended to leave larger tips.

## Discussion

These results support the idea that tips rise with the size of the bill, although the correlation is far from perfect, so habits and other factors also shape how much people tip. Because the data come from a single restaurant and correlation does not establish causation, future research should test whether the pattern holds across restaurants and whether variables such as party size or time of day explain part of it.
